plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a single planar point set with its convex hull traced as a thick gray polygon. Five hull vertices appear as filled black dots and are labeled p_0 at the bottom left, p_1 at the lower right, p_2 at the right, p_3 at the top, and p_4 at the left; eight further black dots lie scattered inside the polygon, joined to nothing. A dashed straight line passes through p_0 and continues upward through p_3; at both of those vertices a pair of short arrows straddles the dashed line, reading left chain with an arrow pointing left and right chain with an arrow pointing right. Every hull vertex also carries a short vertical tick and a horizontal reference ray: at p_0, p_1, and p_2 the ray points right, and a thin arc sweeps from it around to the next hull edge, the arc at p_0 being very narrow and the one at p_2 close to a half turn. At p_4 and p_3 the ray points left instead, with arcs swept from it the same way. The arcs are the quantities being compared, since the next vertex along the boundary is the one subtending the smallest such angle. The picture lays out the wrapping order in which hull vertices are discovered, first up the right chain to the highest point and then back down the left.

interactionPlan.concept: Jarvis's march (gift wrapping) builds the convex hull by repeatedly sweeping a reference ray from the current hull vertex and selecting the point that subtends the smallest polar angle; the reference direction reverses at the topmost and bottommost vertices, splitting the boundary into a right chain and a left chain.

interactions.teaches: At each hull vertex the reference ray sweeps and the next boundary point is the one with the smallest polar angle; stepping vertex by vertex makes the wrapping order p0→p1→p2→p3→p4→p0 explicit

interactions.label: Chain

demo_steps.title: Start at p0 (right chain)
demo_steps.narration: From the lowest point p0 the reference ray points right; sweeping upward, p1 subtends the smallest polar angle, so it becomes the next hull vertex.

demo_steps.title: Wrap up the right chain
demo_steps.narration: Repeating the smallest-angle sweep from p1 then p2 advances the hull to p2 and then to the topmost vertex p3, tracing the right chain.

demo_steps.title: Reference flips at the top
demo_steps.narration: At p3 the reference ray reverses to point left; the same wrapping rule now selects vertices on the opposite side, beginning the left chain.

demo_steps.title: Close the hull on the left chain
demo_steps.narration: Sweeping leftward from p3 picks p4, and one more sweep returns to p0, closing the polygon and completing both chains.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The convex hull is grown one vertex at a time by always choosing the point with the smallest polar angle from a reference ray, and that reference ray flips direction exactly at the topmost and bottommost points — which is why the boundary naturally decomposes into a right chain and a left chain.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place p0 at lower-left, p1 at lower-right, p2 at far right (mid-height), p3 at top-center, p4 at left (mid-height); connect them with a thick light-gray stroked polygon. Scatter eight small black interior dots loosely across the middle. Draw a thin dashed line through p0 and p3 extending slightly beyond both. At every hull vertex draw a short vertical tick and a horizontal reference ray (rightward at p0,p1,p2; leftward at p3,p4) plus a thin black arc sweeping from that ray to the outgoing hull edge — make the p0 arc very narrow and the p2 arc close to a semicircle to convey the angle comparison. Add 'left chain'/'right chain' arrow pairs straddling the dashed line at p0 and p3. On each march step, highlight the active vertex, its reference ray, its sweep arc, and the chosen next edge in an accent color (e.g. red/orange) while dimming the rest; on chain toggle, emphasize the active half of the polygon and flip the reference-ray direction at p3/p0. Hovering an interior dot should draw a faint candidate ray+arc and a small angle label beside the chosen hull angle.

authoredContext:
Jarvis’s march computes the convex hull of a set Q of points by a technique known as package wrapping (or gift wrapping). The algorithm runs in time O.nh/, where h is the number of vertices of CH.Q/. When h is o.lg n/, Jarvis’s march is asymptotically faster than Graham’s scan. Intuitively, Jarvis’s march simulates wrapping a taut piece of paper around the set Q. We start by taping the end of the paper to the lowest point in the set, that is, to the same point p0 with which we start Graham’s scan. We know that this point must be a vertex of the convex hull. We pull the paper to the right to make it taut, and then we pull it higher until it touches a point. This point must also be a vertex of the convex hull. Keeping the paper taut, we continue in this way around the set of vertices until we come back to our original point p0. More formally, Jarvis’s march builds a sequence H D hp0; p1; : : : ; ph1i of the vertices of CH.Q/. We start with p0. As Figure 33.9 shows, the next vertex p1 in the convex hull has the smallest polar angle with respect to p0. (In case of ties, we choose the point farthest from p0.) Similarly, p2 has the smallest polar angle with respect to p1, and so on. When we reach the highest vertex, say pk (breaking
ties by choosing the farthest such vertex), we have constructed, as Figure 33.9
shows, the right chain of CH.Q/. To construct the left chain, we start at pk and
choose pkC1 as the point with the smallest polar angle with respect to pk, but from
the negative x-axis. We continue on, forming the left chain by taking polar angles
from the negative x-axis, until we come back to our original vertex p0.
We could implement Jarvis’s march in one conceptual sweep around the convex
hull, that is, without separately constructing the right and left chains. Such implementations typically keep track of the angle of the last convex-hull side chosen and
require the sequence of angles of hull sides to be strictly increasing (in the range
of 0 to 2_x0019_ radians). The advantage of constructing separate chains is that we need
not explicitly compute angles; the techniques of Section 33.1 suffice to compare
angles.
If implemented properly, Jarvis’s march has a running time of O.nh/. For each
of the h vertices of CH.Q/, we find the vertex with the minimum polar angle. Each
comparison between polar angles takes O.1/ time, using the techniques of Section 33.1. As Section 9.1 shows, we can compute the minimum of n values in O.n/
time if each comparison takes O.1/ time. Thus, Jarvis’s march takes O.nh/ time.

discrepancies: In the default (step-0) state the edge p0–p1 is drawn in bright red/orange and the entire left chain (p3–p4, p4–p0) plus all non-active vertex apparatus are faded to ~0.3–0.4 opacity, whereas the source shows every hull edge as uniform thick gray with black outline and every vertex's tick/ray/arc fully black — the default does not read as a drop-in static replacement.
The 'left chain' / 'right chain' labels are dimmed to 0.35 opacity in the default right-chain state, while the source renders both chain labels (and their arrows) at full weight.
Vertex labels p1–p4 and their reference rays/arcs are faded by default; the source draws all five vertex apparatuses at equal full strength with no emphasis hierarchy.
The auto-docked control panel consumes the right ~third of the canvas, so the pentagon is noticeably smaller and left-shifted compared to the source's full-bleed composition.
evaluation.notes: Topology, vertex positions, interior dots, dashed p0–p3 line, reference rays, sweep arcs and chain arrows are all structurally faithful and the march/chain-toggle/step-player/hover interactions are conceptually correct, but the default state's red edge highlight and heavy dimming of the left chain and non-active vertices make it look unlike the uniform static source.
action_items: Render the initial paint with all hull edges uniform gray and all vertex apparatus and both chain labels at full opacity, matching the static source; apply the red edge highlight and chain/vertex dimming only after the user actually clicks 'Step the march' or toggles the chain checkbox.
Keep non-active vertex labels and the inactive chain's 'left/right chain' text at opacity 1 (or near-1) in the default state so legibility and hierarchy match the source.
Reduce the control panel's footprint (or let the SVG use the full container width) so the pentagon fills the frame as in the source.

feedback.rationale: The concept, geometry, and interactivity are all correct (scores of 4), but the generator applied highlight colors and opacity dimming in the default state instead of reserving them for post-interaction states — these are straightforward implementation fixes to initial rendering state and layout sizing.
